title: Data for Afghanistan: Latest Poverty Lines by Afghanistan Provinces, October 2026
summary: Country: Afghanistan Source: Data for Afghanistan Please refer to the attached file. Summary: Data for Afghanistan estimates that as of October 2026, the average monthly poverty line per person is 2,799 Afghanis . This comprises 1,670 Afghanis for food items and 1,129 Afghanis for non-food items. See the attached full report for provincial poverty lines. Methodology: Baseline poverty lines: Poverty lines are drawn from Afghanistan's Income, Expenditure and Labour Force Survey 2020 (IE&LFS; 2020), conducted by the National Statistics and Information Authority (NSIA) and the World Bank. Poverty lines are estimated per person per month. The food poverty line is set at the cost of obtaining 2,100 kcal per person per day from a reference basket reflecting actual Afghan food consumption, priced at Central Urban (Kabul) prices in Q1 2019 (October–December 2019). Its value was AFN 1,330 per person per month. Non-food poverty lines are area-specific (14 areas covering 8 regions × urban/rural residence) and priced in Q1 2019 (October–December 2019) prices at the time of the survey (IE&LFS; 2020). South and West Central regions are classified as rural-only and have no urban poverty line. As NSIA publishes CPI data only for 20 provinces, we fill missing provinces' CPI with average provincial CPI by region. Please see the attached PDF report for more details on methodology.

title: UNHCR Albania Fact Sheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Albania, Serbia, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. UNHCR advocates for a strengthened national asylum system and contributes to further developing the capacity of government authorities to align asylum laws and practices with international and EU law. UNHCR works with municipalities to strengthen the socio-economic inclusion of refugees and asylum-seekers by improving access to livelihoods, social protection and local services. UNHCR’s work in Albania is supported by the EU-funded EU4Migration project and the PSMM3 Regional Programme. HIGHLIGHTS Socio-economic inclusion UNHCR continues to work with the municipalities of Korça and Gjirokastra to strengthen the socio-economic inclusion of refugees and asylum-seekers. This collaboration aims to address barriers to decent livelihoods and access to social protection rights and schemes. UNHCR also advocates for their inclusion in the local social care systems of both municipalities. Strengthening asylum decision-making In July 2026, UNHCR organized a workshop on drafting asylum decisions to strengthen authorities’ practical skills in fact-finding, credibility assessment and legal analysis. The workshop helped participants develop the skills needed to draft legally sound, well-reasoned and evidence-based decisions. It also promoted exchanges of experience and a shared understanding of asylum decision-making standards among participating institutions.

title: UNHCR Belarus Factsheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Belarus, Afghanistan, Georgia, Ukraine Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. Access to asylum: UNHCR works towards enhancing the asylum space and standardization of the state Refugee Status Determination Procedure (SRSDP) through capacity building and liaison with asylum authorities at country and regional levels. Self-reliance and inclusion: UNHCR promotes inclusive and sustainable integration aligned with the UN Country Framework 2026–2030, aiming to expand the access of forcibly displaced and stateless people to national social protection systems. Since 1 January 2026, UNHCR’s operations in Belarus and the Russian Federation have been consolidated under a Multi‑Country Office (MCO). HIGHLIGHTS UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework On 23 June, the MFA of Belarus and the UN Country Team gathered to present to both the diplomatic community and the business sector in Belarus, strategic directions of their commitments and priorities in accordance with the five-year UNSDCF. UNHCR presented its priorities, focusing on longterm solutions for integration, emphasizing the role of the private sector to support inclusion of refugees in economic activities and promote self-reliance. Protection Monitoring Missions In 2026, UNHCR conducted three field missions across Belarus to monitor the protection situation, engage with regional authorities and learn first-hand information from refugees and asylum-seekers. These missions included visits to state-run accommodation centres for asylum-seekers in Vitebsk and Gomel, as well as a joint mission with the State Border Committee to the Brest region at the Belarus–Poland border.

title: UNHCR Cyprus Factsheet, September 2026
summary: Countries: Cyprus, Cameroon, Democratic Republic of the Congo, occupied Palestinian territory, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees Please refer to the attached file. UNHCR provides legal and technical advice, monitors the asylum system and supports protection-sensitive implementation of the EU Pact. In the northern part of Cyprus, where no formal asylum system exists, UNHCR conducts RSD under its mandate and works with partners to help refugees and asylumseekers access their rights. Across the island, UNHCR maintains direct communication with refugee communities and supports access to legal counselling, psychosocial assistance, promoting inclusion and selfreliance. UNHCR works across Cyprus to ensure access to international protection, prevent refoulement and promote the rights of forcibly displaced and stateless people. HIGHLIGHTS Implementing major asylum reforms Cyprus is moving from policy design to implementation of the EU Pact. UNHCR provides legal advice during the adoption of the legislation and targeted training to asylum service officers, social workers, the judiciary, police and other key stakeholders to support fair, efficient and protection-sensitive asylum processes. Preserving legal and social counselling UNHCR is working with the Government to maintain essential counselling during institutional transition, helping avoid service gaps and ensure continued access to information, referrals and support. Supporting self-reliance At Kofinou Reception Centre, UNHCR supports the transition from reception to independent living through counselling, employment support and housing assistance, strengthening inclusion and easing pressure on the reception system. Building public support for refugee protection Through World Refugee Day initiatives and activities for the 75th anniversary of the Refugee Convention, UNHCR supported community activities across Cyprus that promoted refugee participation, social cohesion and understanding of refugee protection.

title: WFP Indonesia Country Brief, September 2026
summary: Country: Indonesia Source: World Food Programme Please refer to the attached file. KEY HIGHLIGHTS • WFP advanced technical support to Indonesia’s Free Nutritious Meals Programme, through cooperative guidance, fortified-rice policy and costing, beneficiary-targeting consultations, and South-South learning with Brazil and other partners. It secured government consensus on the fortified-rice costing study approach and institutional commitments for the next phase, while strengthening cooperative readiness, food safety and supply continuity. • WFP supported national and subnational institutionalization of Anticipatory Action through Aksi Merespon Peringatan Dini (AMPD; Early Warning Response Action), advancing the National AMPD Strategy and Guideline, Gunungkidul’s drought protocol and financing arrangements, and drought preparedness and village capacity in East Nusa Tenggara (NTT). • Gunungkidul operationalized its anticipatory action protocol and obtained legal clearance for a draft financing regulation, pending harmonization. In NTT, WFP and partners assessed six priority districts’ readiness, supported protocol guidance, began forecasting collaboration and launched village training for drought preparedness. SITUATION OVERVIEW • Indonesia is an upper-middle-income country with an annual gross national income of USD 5,120 per capita (World Bank, 2025). Despite substantial gains in poverty reduction and food security, alongside efforts to reduce inequality, malnutrition remains a concern. • Indonesia ranks 70th of 123 countries in the 2025 Global Hunger Index. Undernourishment fell from 7.2 percent in 2024 to 6.3 percent in 2025. The 2025 Food Security and Vulnerability Atlas identifies 62 of 514 districts/municipalities as vulnerable to food insecurity. • Gross domestic product grew 5.29 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, while inflation had risen to 4.76 by February 2026. Food price pressures persist, particularly for volatile commodities. The ongoing El Niño is heightening drought risks and threatening agricultural production and food availability. • In 2025, Indonesia experienced about 4,727 environmental and extreme weather disasters—36percent higher than in 2024. Most were due to climate anomalies, impacting over 12 million people. • WFP Indonesia engages in policy dialogue and provides technical assistance to the Government of Indonesia in the context of food security, school meals, and climate and disaster risk management.

title: Flash floods cut families off from healthcare in Mudug, Somalia
summary: Country: Somalia Source: Médecins Sans Frontières Flash flooding from heavy Deyr rains has affected more than 20,000 households in Galmudug, including in Galkayo, according to the state authorities. In Galkayo, floodwater has cut roads across the town, making it harder and more expensive for families to reach MSF-supported Mudug Regional Hospital and Galkayo TB Hospital. Cases of acute watery diarrhoea at MSF-supported facilities in Mudug more than doubled, from 356 in October 2025 to 748 in October 2026, and two cholera cases have been confirmed at Mudug Regional Hospital. Nearly two in three children admitted to the inpatient malnutrition ward in early November had acute watery diarrhoea. Our teams have expanded the ward from 28 to 70 beds, strengthened disease surveillance, trained staff on cholera, dengue and measles, and are reinforcing our capacity to treat cholera cases. ​ Flash floods are hitting towns across central Somalia, yet flood preparedness and limited available funding focus mainly on river flooding. Repairs In places such as Mudug, resources for responding to flash floods remain insufficient, leaving little for the drainage, safe water and sanitation that would protect families’ access to healthcare through the next rains. Humanitarian funding cuts are also leaving families across Somalia further from care. MSF calls on donors to make flexible funding available for the wider response to flash floods in areas such as Mudug, not only to riverine floods. MSF also calls on health authorities and humanitarian organisations to strengthen a coordinated response to urgent health, water and sanitation needs, and to invest in health facilities that can keep functioning through future floods. Families in Galkayo should not lose access to healthcare because the flood that reached them came from heavy rain rather than a river. For 15 days, Farhia Hassan Aden’s 18-month-old son had been vomiting and had diarrhoea. There is no clinic in her village in Mudug region, and since the October rains the motorised rickshaws that carry families to hospital have not been able to get through the water. The fare, US$4 to 5, was more than the family could pay. So Farhia walked through the floodwater with her son to Mudug Regional Hospital in Galkayo, which Doctors Without Borders/ Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) supports. He was admitted. “It forced us to walk in the water with our sick children,” she says. Farhia’s family is one of many caught by flash flooding since the Deyr rains began in October, in a year of El Niño conditions. In one week in October, more than 20,000 households were affected across Galmudug, including in Galkayo district, according to the authorities. Cut off and falling ill For five days, Bisharo Badal Yusuf could not get her 14-month-old son to hospital. He was vomiting and had diarrhoea, but floodwater had cut the roads. “We are cut off, which has forced families to keep sick children at home,” she says. “I eventually brought him to the hospital in critical condition.” Two days into his treatment, his fever had come down. Standing floodwater is also making people ill. Toilets have overflowed, floodwater has mixed with sewage, and the stagnant water that collects between houses fills with flies and mosquitoes. “The children are constantly scratching, and insects are swarming around them,” says Farhia. What our teams are seeing In October 2026, our teams recorded 748 cases of acute watery diarrhoea at MSF-supported facilities in Mudug, more than double the 356 in October 2025. Some patients have travelled more than 200 kilometres for care. In early November, admissions to the inpatient malnutrition ward at Mudug Regional Hospital were almost double last year’s, and nearly two in three children admitted had acute watery diarrhoea. We have expanded the ward from 28 to 70 beds. MSF works alongside the Ministry of Health at Mudug Regional Hospital and Galkayo Hospital, supporting emergency, maternity, neonatal and paediatric care, treatment for children with severe acute malnutrition, tuberculosis care and community health activities, all free of charge. Since the rains began, we have added staff, strengthened disease surveillance, trained teams on cholera, dengue and measles, and put supplies in place. Two cholera cases have now been confirmed at Mudug Regional Hospital. With the health authorities, our teams are strengthening cholera case management and sending mobile clinics to the communities hit hardest. Fewer places to turn For a family that, in Farhia’s words, “cannot even afford a single tablet of medicine”, each closure means a longer journey and a higher fare, and free care far away can be out of reach even before the roads flood. “Funding has been shrinking across the whole of Somalia, and access to healthcare with it,” says Dr Janvier Bahati, MSF project medical referent in Mudug. “In the long run, El Niño will make the current situation worse, reducing people’s capacity to cope, to the point where they are vulnerable to disease and malnutrition.” What families are asking for Asked what would help, the mothers we spoke to named simple things. Farhia wants the mosquitoes sprayed and the floodwater pumped out. Bisharo wants sanitation improved and “channels for the water”. “What the humanitarian actors need to focus on is to make sure that communities far away, and those affected by the flood, also have access to services,” says Bahati. “For me, that is the call: a drainage system across the city, chlorination of water and distribution of Aquatabs at community level.” Yet flood preparedness has focused largely on the river basins, leaving little for drainage, safe water and sanitation in places such as Mudug. MSF calls on donors to make flexible funding available for the wider response to flash floods in areas such as Mudug, not only to riverine floods. MSF also calls on health authorities and humanitarian organisations to strengthen a coordinated response to urgent health, water and sanitation needs, and to invest in health facilities that can keep functioning through future floods. title: Somalia: Radio Ergo Weekly Feedback Report, Issued: 27 Nov 2026
summary: Country: Somalia Source: Radio Ergo Please refer to the attached file. Brief Summary Commentary on rainfall and its positive impact on lives and livelihoods continued to form the bulk of the calls to Radio Ergo’s nationwide feedback platform in the week 19-25 November 2026. These calls came mostly from Jubbaland, South West, Hirshabelle, and some from Galmudug. However, some callers mainly in southern locations noted a tailing off of the rainfall, patchy areas without rain, and also intensely hot temperatures. A few in Gedo and Bay regions said they were now running short of water again. Drought conditions were cited in Bari. Several callers complained about influxes of mosquitoes and rising malaria cases, and wanted mosquito control measures. In Gedo region a number of IDP callers complained of hardships and their need for aid. The following summarises the calls by theme. Health – callers in Awdhegle in Lower Shabelle and Adado in Galgadud spoke of influxes of mosquitoes in their areas and a rise in malaria and wanted the menace to be brought under control. A caller in Gedo said the mosquitoes were causing illness with headaches and fever. A caller in Bardera said they had good rainfall, but mosquitoes were their main concern. A caller in Dollow also cited a mosquito influx, adding that despite the rain people were impoverished and aid agencies hadn’t visited the area for six months. IDPs – a caller in Iftin camp, Bardera, said they and their farms were doing well after the rain. On the other hand, a female caller in Bardera identifying as an IDP said they had received little rainfall, their crops had been attacked by pests and disease, and the schools had been shut for the past six months depriving the children of education. In Qurdubey, a caller called twice on behalf of displaced families who had lost their livestock. He said those families with a few livestock left were able to sell them for a living, but others like them were facing hardship and challenging conditions including poor sanitation. He added an appeal for aid. Aid – a caller in Dollow complained that they had been registered by aid groups a few days ago, but had not received the cash aid they thought they were going to get. Another caller, location unspecified, wanted a resumption of the cash aid they used to get from WFP that had stopped. Food Security – a caller in Bardera said he wanted to share information about the high inflation and rising costs of basics they were facing. Locusts – a caller in Kismayo said he had a farm near the airport and was concerned about locusts. He wanted to know how the farmers could protect their crops. Climate – a caller in Baidoa, Bay region, said they’d been experiencing intense heat and wanted to know if this was because of climate change. Similarly, a caller in Bahdo, Galgadud, said recent days had been intensely hot and people wondered if it was a sign of rain to come, or of climate change. Other callers in Guriel, Dollow, and Kismayo also described intense heat in their areas. Agriculture – farmers in southern and some central areas complained of pests damaging a range of produce including potatoes, beans, sesame, sorghum, maize, lettuce and tomatoes. They wanted to talk with experts on Radio Ergo’s weekly farming programme. Livestock – a caller in Bardera said his camels had dukan (trypanosomiasis) and the medicine he was injecting them with was not working. He wanted veterinary advice. Several herders in Jubbaland complained of foot and mouth affecting their herds. A caller in Beletweyne wanted to know more about how pre-export livestock inspections and certifications were processed in Somalia. Drought & water shortage – a caller in Rako-raho, Bari region, said they faced drought in the area and that many people had already migrated away. He added that they were in a desperate situation and needed the Puntland authority to reach them with aid. One caller in Dusamareb said they faced drought and conflict. Several in Bay region said the rain had been poor or had stopped already, with one describing the drying up of crops and grazing. A caller in Bardera said rainfall had been little and their farms were failing due to water shortages. A female caller said that odder and water shortage were affecting their livestock. Another female caller in Lower Juba said they weren’t having rainfall, the heat was intense, and their livestock were struggling. Rainfall – a female caller in Farjeni, Bari, said they had received some light rain. A caller in Harardhere, Mudug, said they were getting heavy rain and doing well. In Galgadud, callers spoke of decent rain in Bahdo, Guriel, Abudwak, and Adado, with several noting intense heat. In Hiran, callers in Buleburte, Af-ad, and El-gal noted good rain and conditions for their livestock and farms. Callers in Baidoa, Burhakaba, and Dinsor in Bay region cited beneficial rain. One in Bakool said the rain was short-lived and they hoped for more. In Gedo, several in different districts said they had had good rain but that in some places it had stopped. A caller in Tulo-banan said the rain was good, although they were poor and there were no jobs. A number of callers in Kismayo cited beneficial rainfall helping crops and livestock, while some noted dry areas nearby.

title: South Sudan Humanitarian Fund: 2026 monitoring report (1 January to 31 August 2026)
summary: Countries: South Sudan, Sudan Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached file. South Sudan Humanitarian Fund: 2026 monitoring report (1 January to 31 August 2026) The South Sudan Humanitarian Fund (SSHF) monitored 87 projects implemented by 54 partners from 1 January to 31 August 2026. The report describes how partners delivered assistance and managed funds, what delayed delivery and how the Fund follows up on problems it finds. At a glance 87 projects monitored: 43 implemented by national non-governmental organizations, 33 by international non-governmental organizations and 11 by United Nations agencies 54 implementing partners: 30 national non-governmental organizations, 19 international non-governmental organizations and five United Nations agencies 142 monitoring exercises: 77 field visits, 20 remote assessments (11 calls and nine surveys) and 45 on-site financial spot-checks What the monitoring found SSHF rated 71 of 97 field visits and remote assessments (73 per cent) good or outstanding. In 23 assessments, operating conditions justified underperformance. In two, the justification was insufficient. In one, no project activity had taken place at the time of monitoring. These ratings reflect what monitors found at the time of each assessment. For an overall assessment of project performance, the Fund also considers financial spot-checks, partner reports, cluster reports and other evidence. SSHF rated 38 of 45 financial spot-checks (84 per cent) good or outstanding. Six found underperformance with sufficient justification and one without. The checks identified gaps in supporting documents, procurement procedures, personnel records, expenditure coding and internal controls. In one case, a payment voucher lacked a delivery note and a goods received note. A follow-up spot-check confirmed that the partner had filed both documents with the voucher. Community committees helped partners identify people in need of assistance and resolve disputes. Providing health, nutrition, protection and water, sanitation and hygiene services together improved access and referrals. Mobile teams helped reach displaced people and remote communities. Delayed or incomplete supplies disrupted delivery. Flooding and insecurity restricted access, delayed construction and raised costs. Inflation reduced what people could buy with cash assistance. Follow-up The Fund will work with clusters and supply agencies to address delays, train national partners in financial management and reporting, track corrective actions, improve monitoring data and documentation, and complete the remaining monitoring planned for 2026. It will use the findings to inform partner risk assessments, project revisions and future funding allocations.

title: Sudan: El Niño suma nuevos puntos críticos del hambre mientras los conflictos siguen aumentando el riesgo de hambruna, advierten la FAO y WFP
summary: Countries: Sudan, Central African Republic, Chad, Eswatini, Guatemala, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mozambique, Myanmar, Nigeria, Somalia, South Sudan, Yemen, Zambia, Zimbabwe Sources: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, World Food Programme Sudán, Sudán del Sur, Somalia, algunas zonas de Nigeria y Yemen siguen siendo los puntos críticos de máxima preocupación, mientras que África austral y el Corredor Seco Centroamericano figuran entre las nuevas incorporaciones. ROMA – El Niño ha llevado a África austral y al Corredor Seco Centroamericano a la lista de puntos críticos del hambre, donde se prevé que la inseguridad alimentaria aguda empeore significativamente entre diciembre de 2026 y mayo de 2027, advirtieron hoy la Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO) y el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas (WFP). En su último informe Hunger Hotspots (Puntos críticos del hambre) , los organismos también identificaron un riesgo de hambruna en algunas zonas de Sudán y Sudán del Sur. El informe, publicado dos veces al año a través de la Red Mundial contra las Crisis Alimentarias, identifica 16 puntos críticos, frente a los 13 registrados en junio. El Niño es uno de los principales factores detrás de tres de los cuatro nuevos puntos críticos identificados: África austral (Eswatini, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia y Zimbabwe), el Corredor Seco Centroamericano y el noreste de Uganda. Chad se ha incorporado a la lista debido a los efectos persistentes del conflicto en el vecino Sudán. El Niño está cobrando fuerza y podría convertirse en uno de los más intensos jamás registrados. En África austral, las condiciones más secas y cálidas amenazan las siembras, las labores agrícolas y las futuras cosechas. Se prevé que hasta 3 millones de personas en Zimbabwe, 2,6 millones en Malawi y 1,8 millones en Mozambique enfrenten altos niveles de inseguridad alimentaria aguda en los próximos meses, hasta marzo de 2027 En el Corredor Seco Centroamericano, la temporada de Primera de 2026 fue la más seca en cuatro décadas y las pérdidas de cultivos superaron el 75 por ciento en muchas zonas. A medida que se agotan las reservas de alimentos, la temporada de escasez de 2027 podría comenzar antes de lo habitual. Solo en Guatemala, se prevé que 3,2 millones de personas enfrenten altos niveles de inseguridad alimentaria aguda entre octubre de 2026 y febrero de 2027. Actuar antes de que lleguen los peores efectos de El Niño puede evitar daños a las cosechas, el ganado y los medios de vida. El plan conjunto de acción anticipatoria de la FAO y WFP frente a El Niño tiene como objetivo proteger a 9 millones de personas en 22 países. En otras regiones, los conflictos y la violencia armada siguen figurando entre los principales factores que impulsan la inseguridad alimentaria aguda en 12 de los 16 puntos críticos, incluidos los cinco puntos críticos de máxima preocupación: Sudán, Sudán del Sur, Somalia, algunas zonas de Nigeria y Yemen. En cuatro de estos cinco puntos críticos, los análisis más recientes identificaron o proyectaron poblaciones en situación de Catástrofe, la fase más grave de la Clasificación Integrada de la Seguridad Alimentaria en Fases (CIF), caracterizada por la inanición y la muerte. En Somalia, aunque actualmente no se prevé que ninguna población enfrente una situación de Catástrofe (Fase 5 de la CIF) y el riesgo de hambruna ha disminuido, la inseguridad alimentaria aguda se mantiene en niveles de Emergencia (Fase 4 de la CIF) entre las poblaciones desplazadas en Baidoa. Las situaciones más graves se registran en Sudán y Sudán del Sur, donde se ha identificado un riesgo de hambruna. Bajo un escenario razonable de máxima gravedad, existe riesgo de hambruna en 13 zonas de Darfur del Norte y Kordofán del Sur, en Sudán, hasta enero de 2027, mientras que en dos campamentos para personas desplazadas en Darfur del Sur los niveles de malnutrición aguda ya han superado los umbrales de hambruna. En Sudán del Sur, el último análisis disponible indicó un riesgo de hambruna en cuatro condados de los estados de Alto Nilo y Jonglei hasta julio de 2026, bajo un escenario de máxima gravedad. Los cinco puntos críticos de máxima preocupación se han mantenido reiteradamente en este nivel desde 2022. Sin embargo, la financiación destinada a la asistencia humanitaria para la seguridad alimentaria y la nutrición en estos puntos críticos cayó un 62 por ciento, de USD 5.100 millones en 2022 a USD 2.000 millones en 2025. Otros cuatro puntos críticos están clasificados como de muy alta preocupación : Afganistán, la República Democrática del Congo, Haití y Palestina. Aunque la seguridad alimentaria en la Franja de Gaza ha comenzado a mejorar tras el alto el fuego de octubre de 2025, los avances son frágiles y se prevé que la inseguridad alimentaria aguda empeore en Cisjordania. La FAO y WFP hacen un llamado a adoptar medidas humanitarias urgentes en los 16 puntos críticos, sobre todo allí donde se ha identificado un riesgo de hambruna, y a garantizar un acceso seguro y sin obstáculos a las personas que necesitan asistencia. “El Niño se está intensificando, amenazando los cultivos y las cosechas en regiones que ya son vulnerables y aumentando el riesgo de inseguridad alimentaria aguda”, afirmó el Director General de la FAO, QU Dongyu. “Sin embargo, los peores escenarios no son inevitables. La asistencia agrícola que salva vidas, destinada a impulsar la producción de alimentos de las familias altamente vulnerables, es una parte esencial de la respuesta multisectorial a las situaciones descritas en el informe. Ahí es donde la FAO está centrando sus esfuerzos”. “He hecho un llamado a todas las naciones para desterrar la hambruna a los libros de historia”, afirmó el Director Ejecutivo de WFP, Luke J. Lindberg. “Este informe nos indica dónde podría producirse la próxima hambruna, por lo que el momento de cumplir nuestro compromiso es ahora. Será necesario un esfuerzo conjunto para poner fin a los conflictos, dotar de todos los recursos necesarios a nuestros equipos de WFP sobre el terreno y garantizar que tengan acceso seguro para llegar a las comunidades vulnerables. No se trata de un problema de capacidad operativa, sino de si los líderes mundiales tienen el valor político para actuar con decisión”. # # # Los 16 puntos críticos del hambre Máxima preocupación: Sudán, Sudán del Sur, Somalia, algunas zonas de Nigeria y Yemen. Muy alta preocupación: Afganistán, República Democrática del Congo, Haití y Palestina. Otros puntos críticos: Chad, Corredor Seco Centroamericano, Madagascar, Malí, Myanmar, África austral (Eswatini, Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia y Zimbabwe) y el noreste de Uganda. Chad, el Corredor Seco Centroamericano, África austral y el noreste de Uganda son nuevas incorporaciones a la lista. Líbano ya no figura como punto crítico. Nota sobre las fases de la CIF La Fase 3 de la CIF se refiere a niveles de “Crisis” de inseguridad alimentaria, en los que los hogares presentan brechas en el consumo de alimentos que se reflejan en niveles altos o superiores a los habituales de malnutrición aguda, o apenas pueden satisfacer sus necesidades alimentarias mínimas, pero solo agotando activos esenciales para sus medios de vida o recurriendo a estrategias de afrontamiento de crisis. La Fase 4 de la CIF se refiere a niveles de “Emergencia” de inseguridad alimentaria, en los que los hogares presentan grandes brechas en el consumo de alimentos, reflejadas en niveles muy altos de malnutrición aguda y exceso de mortalidad, o logran mitigar estas brechas únicamente mediante estrategias de emergencia relacionadas con sus medios de vida y la liquidación de activos. La Fase 5 de la CIF se refiere a niveles de “Catástrofe/Hambruna”, en los que los hogares enfrentan una carencia extrema de alimentos y/o de otras necesidades básicas incluso después de emplear plenamente sus estrategias de afrontamiento. Son evidentes la inanición, la muerte, la indigencia y niveles extremadamente críticos de malnutrición aguda. A nivel de los hogares, la Fase 5 de la CIF se clasifica como Catástrofe, mientras que la hambruna es una clasificación a nivel de área que requiere pruebas de que se han alcanzado los umbrales de inseguridad alimentaria aguda, malnutrición aguda y mortalidad. El Cadre Harmonisé (CH), utilizado en África Occidental y el Sahel, emplea las mismas fases. Notas para los editores Identificados mediante análisis prospectivos, los puntos críticos del hambre son zonas donde es probable que la inseguridad alimentaria aguda se deteriore significativamente durante el período de perspectivas. Se seleccionan mediante un proceso basado en el consenso en el que participan los equipos técnicos y sobre el terreno de la FAO y WFP, junto con analistas especializados en conflictos, riesgos económicos y amenazas naturales. El informe se elabora con el apoyo financiero de la Unión Europea a través de la Red Mundial contra las Crisis Alimentarias. El informe completo puede consultarse aquí . El material de apoyo (B-roll) y la lista de tomas pueden consultarse aquí . Las fotografías pueden consultarse aquí . La Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO) es un organismo especializado que lidera los esfuerzos internacionales para acabar con el hambre. Su objetivo es lograr la seguridad alimentaria para todos y garantizar el acceso regular a suficientes alimentos de alta calidad para llevar una vida activa y saludable. La FAO trabaja en más de 130 países para transformar los sistemas agroalimentarios y hacerlos más eficientes, inclusivos, resilientes y sostenibles. El Programa Mundial de Alimentos de las Naciones Unidas (WFP) es la organización humanitaria más grande del mundo, que salva vidas en situaciones de emergencia y utiliza la asistencia alimentaria para construir un camino hacia la paz, la estabilidad y la prosperidad para las personas que se recuperan de conflictos, desastres y los efectos de fenómenos meteorológicos extremos

title: Sudan: Protection Cluster Alert : Escalating Conflict, Mass Displacement and Protection Risks in Blue Nile State - 27 November 2026
summary: Country: Sudan Sources: Child Protection Area of Responsibility, Gender Based Violence Area of Responsibility, Housing, Land, and Property Area of Responsibility, Mine Action Area of Responsibility, Protection Cluster Please refer to the attached file. The Sudan Protection Cluster is publishing a Protection Alert on the escalating conflict, mass displacement and deteriorating protection situation in Blue Nile State, dated 27 November 2026. The intensification of hostilities since early November has resulted in the displacement of approximately 47,460 individuals, with preliminary reports indicating an additional 22,467 individuals displaced, pending verification. These developments are exacerbating existing vulnerabilities and placing further pressure on already overstretched humanitarian services and reception capacities. The Protection Cluster is deeply concerned about the deteriorating protection environment, particularly threats to civilian life, safety and dignity, repeated displacement, barriers to seeking safety, heightened protection risks for women and children, explosive ordnance contamination, and increasingly constrained access to humanitarian assistance and essential services. The situation also underscores the importance of preserving the civilian and humanitarian character of refugee settlements. The alert presents an analysis of the evolving protection situation, recalls the obligations of all parties to the conflict under international humanitarian law, and outlines priority actions to prevent and mitigate protection risks and strengthen the collective humanitarian response. In light of these developments, the Protection Cluster calls for urgent and coordinated action to: Reinforce collective advocacy for the protection of civilians and safe, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access. Ensure the continuity and scale-up of life-saving protection services. Strengthen protection risk mitigation across all sectors of the humanitarian response. Enhance contingency planning and operational preparedness for further displacement and potential deterioration of humanitarian access. Sustain support for local and community-based responders and safeguard their operational space.

UNHCR is engaged in the development of a new Asylum Strategy 2027 and works with authorities and NGOs to further strengthen the quality of the asylum system and the socio-economic inclusion of refugees. Switzerland remains a strong supporter of UNHCR, both as host of UNHCR’s headquarters and a top donor, providing flexible and predictable multi-year funding. Through the partnership between Path2Work and UNHCR, bridges are being built between refugee talent and employers, creating new career opportunities and laying the foundations for sustainable integration. Access to the labour market fosters self-reliance, inclusion, and meaningful participation in society.

title: The Systems Beneath Recovery: What WASH in Health Reveals About Recovery Readiness in Ukraine
summary: Country: Ukraine Source: WeWorld Please refer to the attached file. What does it take to rebuild a health system that can withstand future shocks, respond to changing needs and provide quality care for everyone? This report explores that question through a lens that is often overlooked in discussions on reconstruction: water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services in healthcare settings. Drawing on nearly five years of WeWorld’s experience in Ukraine, this report argues that WASH in Health is far more than a technical or infrastructure issue. Reliable water supply, sanitation, hygiene, waste management and accessible environments are fundamental to quality care, infection prevention, preparedness and resilience. The findings show that rebuilding infrastructure alone is not enough. Sustainable recovery depends on strong management, adequate funding and regular maintenance, alongside practical tools such as WASH FIT to support planning and decision-making. Resilient healthcare also requires prepared staff, reliable backup systems and accessible, inclusive services, particularly as the needs of persons with disabilities and veterans continue to grow. Ultimately, this publication shows that how essential systems are managed and maintained today will shape the quality and resilience of healthcare in the years to come.

title: World AIDS Day 2026 - Statement by Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director of UNAIDS
summary: Country: World Source: UNAIDS World AIDS Day 2026 is my last as Executive Director of UNAIDS. Today, we remember the nearly 45 million people we have lost to AIDS and we stand in solidarity with the 41 million people living with HIV and with the communities who have carried this response forward with courage, determination and love. In reflecting on the past and looking to the future, I feel both immense pride and deep concern. Pride in what has been achieved through science, solidarity and struggle. Concern that, at the very moment when we have the tools to end AIDS, political choices and deepening inequalities threaten to put that goal beyond our reach. Thirty years of progress, struggle and solidarity I remember when an HIV diagnosis was effectively a death sentence. Today, 32.1 million people are receiving life-saving treatment, including 29 million in developing countries. This extraordinary achievement represents a collective victory. A victory for people living with HIV who refused to accept that their lives were worth less than those of others. For activists who challenged the power of pharmaceutical corporations and held governments to account for realising rights. For communities who confronted prejudice and discrimination. And for governments that recognised their shared responsibility to end a global health crisis. For decades, the AIDS movement has challenged the inequalities that drive AIDS. Science must translate into access Today, science has brought us to another turning point. Lenacapavir, an HIV prevention injection administered just twice a year, could transform our ability to prevent new infections. By June of this year, more than 50,000 people in nine sub-Saharan African countries had received it. From 2027, generic versions are expected to become available at just US$40 per person per year in eligible lower-income countries. Other long-acting prevention and treatment technologies are advancing rapidly. Imagine what these innovations could mean for adolescent girls and young women in Africa, who continue to face an unacceptable burden of new HIV infections. But I have learned one lesson from decades of fighting inequality: a scientific breakthrough is not a public health breakthrough until it reaches the people who need it. That is why, this World AIDS Day, our message is simple: ending AIDS starts with access. Access is about rights and justice Access is about more than the simple existence of a clinic or a treatment. It is about whether medicines are affordable. Whether a person living with HIV can receive treatment without stigma or discrimination Whether a young woman has the power to protect herself. Whether a gay man can seek health care without fear of arrest. Whether a sex worker can enter a clinic without humiliation. Whether activists and communities can organise and gather to protest, demand change, and achieve solidarity. Access is about power, rights and justice. And today, all three are under attack. We cannot allow progress to be reversed The global AIDS response has been shaken by a financing shock of historic proportions. International HIV assistance fell by 18% in 2025, and the annual financing gap in developing countries now stands at US$4.3 billion. The latest UNAIDS report reveals the scale of the damage. Across countries reporting data, around 446,000 fewer people received oral HIV prevention medicines in 2025 than in 2024. Worldwide, 300 million fewer condoms were distributed. In priority countries, the number of voluntary medical male circumcisions fell by more than half. It is unconscionable that, just as science is expanding the possibilities for HIV prevention, access to even the most established prevention tools is being eroded. And the worst consequences of these cuts still lie ahead. Today's figures cannot yet tell us the full story of the lives that will be affected by the decisions taken over the past two years. A young woman who fails to access prevention today may acquire HIV tomorrow. A person who loses the support they need to stay on treatment may become seriously ill in the months ahead. We must act now, before these setbacks translate into needless HIV infections and AIDS-related deaths. I am particularly concerned about the dismantling of community-led services. Community organisations have been among the first to lose funding, even as organised anti-rights movements are making their work more difficult and, in some places, more dangerous. These are the organisations that have spent decades building trust with people whom health systems have too often failed. They have reached the most marginalised communities, helped people access prevention and treatment, and defended their right to health. Once lost, that infrastructure, that knowledge, those relationships and that trust cannot easily be rebuilt. At the same time, we are witnessing attacks on gender equality, sexual and reproductive health and rights, and the rights of LGBTQ+ people. Civic space is shrinking. Discriminatory laws and policies are driving people away from health services. We cannot end AIDS while denying people their rights. And we cannot protect the gains of the AIDS response while dismantling the community organisations that made those gains possible. Countries must have the means to lead The financing crisis has forced an overdue conversation about the future of the AIDS response. I welcome the growing determination of countries to strengthen national ownership, increase domestic investment and integrate HIV services into inclusive, rights-based national health systems. UNAIDS has recorded increases in domestic HIV expenditure in 55 countries. Those governments’ leadership deserves recognition and support. But national ownership cannot mean abandoning international solidarity. In many countries heavily affected by HIV, debt servicing outstrips public spending on health. This means that scarce revenues are being diverted to pay creditors while organisations are operating on the breadline and individuals are vulnerable. We cannot expect countries to replace aid financing overnight. And we cannot demand that governments invest more in their people's health while tolerating an international financial architecture that denies them the resources to do so. We need debt relief and fairer international financing rules. We need a planned transition away from aid, while countries build nationally owned and sustainably financed HIV responses. And we need to reform the rules governing intellectual property so that publicly supported scientific innovation serves the public good, rather than allowing monopolies and high prices to determine who lives and who dies. These are political choices, driven by interests. But people have confronted interests and changed policies before, and will do again. We can still end AIDS Even in this most challenging of years, I have found reasons for hope. Thirty years ago, UNAIDS was created because the world recognised that defeating AIDS required something different: a joint effort bringing together governments, the United Nations, scientists and communities. That model of solidarity and shared leadership has helped transform the course of the epidemic. This year, 149 countries voted in favour of an ambitious new United Nations Political Declaration on HIV and AIDS. Governments committed to reaching 40 million people with HIV treatment and 20 million with antiretroviral-based prevention by 2030. They committed to mobilising US$21.9 billion annually for the AIDS response in low- and middle-income countries, to defending human rights and gender equality, and to strengthening and financing community leadership. If these commitments are fulfilled, an estimated 3.2 million new HIV infections and 1.3 million AIDS-related deaths could be averted by 2030. On this World AIDS Day, I urge governments to make HIV a national priority, to invest in sustainable, inclusive and rights-based health systems, to remove the legal and social barriers that deny people access to services, and to ensure that communities are resourced and empowered to lead the AIDS response. And I urge the international community to renew, rather than retreat from, its commitment to ending AIDS. As I mark my last World AIDS Day as Executive Director of UNAIDS, I draw strength from the extraordinary courage of the AIDS movement. Throughout my years leading UNAIDS, I have seen people living with HIV, women's movements, LGBTQ+ activists and other community leaders refuse to surrender, even in the most hostile circumstances. They have defended rights, challenged injustice and kept services alive when institutions failed them. They remind us that progress is never inevitable. It must be fought for, and protected against backlash or weakening political will. Ending AIDS requires political courage: to invest in people, defend human rights, confront inequality and put the public good before private profit. The communities most affected by HIV have shown that courage for decades. We have the science. We know what works. We know what stands in our way. The question is no longer whether we can end AIDS. It is whether we will make the choices necessary to do so. We must not fail this generation. Ending AIDS starts with access.

title: World AIDS Day: People still don’t have access to key HIV prevention medicine
summary: Country: World Source: Médecins Sans Frontières Despite generic lenacapavir slowly becoming available for some, Gilead continues to stand in the way of equitable and affordable access amid urgent global need and demand. NEW YORK/JOHANNESBURG, NOVEMBER 26 — In advance of World AIDS Day on December 1, Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is once again calling for more people globally to have access to the highly effective HIV prevention medicine lenacapavir . This twice-yearly injectable version of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is the biggest breakthrough in HIV prevention yet, but US-based Gilead Sciences continues to block affordable access for countries around the world. This includes countries with growing HIV epidemics and ongoing humanitarian crises. As a result of its long-acting nature, lenacapavir may be especially valuable for stigmatized or criminalized populations, who often are excluded from or concerned about accessing health care. It is also a critical tool for people on the move who may struggle to access health clinics, people living in remote areas with few health care options, and people caught in humanitarian emergencies — including those in many of the communities in which MSF operates. “Gilead’s greed alone is the reason people across the globe don’t have access to lenacapavir already,” said Carlota Baptista da Silva, MSF’s global HIV/HCV access and advocacy lead. “Our teams are ready to provide it but have been left empty-handed or with very few doses to offer. We have patients in Eswatini and Zimbabwe ​ who’ve asked for this medicine and have been told it’s not an option because those countries' stocks had already been depleted. Kenya was supposed to see a priority roll-out but instead has faced severe shortages and delays in access. And communities where the lenacapavir clinical trials were held in Brazil, Argentina, Peru, and Mexico haven’t been guaranteed affordable access to it by Gilead.” A generic version of this twice-yearly PrEP made by Indian manufacturer Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) in November. Dr. Reddy’s has agreed to sell its version of lenacapavir for $40 per person per year compared to the more than $28,000 per person per year that Gilead sells it for in the US. The first delivery of generics arrived in Zambia on the 25th November . However, generics won’t be available everywhere; dozens of middle-income countries will not have access to them because of the restrictive terms of Gilead’s licensing agreements . Countries blocked from accessing generics include most of Latin America, where HIV infections rose 25 percent between 2010 and 2025. An agreement Gilead has struck with the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) to supply lenacapavir in Latin America does little to ease concerns about access; the agreement ensures Gilead’s total control over supply in the region without revealing the price it will charge. Without the availability of generic lenacapavir, people in these countries are likely to pay far more than the $40 available elsewhere. “Even with the approval and arrival of generic lenacapavir, Gilead is still dictating which countries can access it and which cannot,” Baptista da Silva said. “The company continues to keep affordable versions of this medicine out of reach for millions by restricting which manufacturers can produce it and where they can sell it. The company could choose to expand the list of countries eligible for affordable generic versions of lenacapavir but is choosing to protect its profits instead. The only way to possibly end AIDS is to increase access to prevention tools like this one." These access gaps come amid recent funding cuts to HIV programs by many key governments, many of which have historically funded global HIV/AIDS efforts. Prevention efforts and services, particularly those targeting stigmatized populations, have been hit the hardest. “Many of our patients are caught in conflict, have been forced from their homes, or live in places with few health care options,” Baptista da Silva said. “Only having to get this medicine twice per year would make it much easier for someone to remain protected against HIV even if they’re on the move or unable to access a medical facility between injections. But they can only do that if it’s available more widely and affordable for them. It’s simply unacceptable that a single pharmaceutical company can dictate who can access this medicine and who can’t.” Lenacapavir must be available for $40 or less in all low- and middle-income countries. Governments must step in to help increase access if Gilead continues to block generics from being sold in more countries. ENDS.
